Police in India's Gujarat publicly beat man accused of killing partner. Indian police publicly thrashed a man accused of beating his partner to death, local media reported on Sunday, drawing mixed reactions after footage of the flogging spread online. Public parading and beatings of suspects by police are not uncommon in India, despite Supreme Court rulings prohibiting such treatment. Officials said the thrashing was a response to the brutality of the alleged murder. The man, identified by police as Faizal Lakhani, was arrested in Bhavnagar, a town in Gujarat state. Police took Lakhani on Friday to the scene of the alleged crime to reconstruct the incident. He was beaten at the site, and footage of the battering was shared widely on social media. Videos show Lakhani’s arms restrained by ropes as a uniformed officer repeatedly struck his legs and buttocks with a bamboo baton. He was also beaten on his feet inside a bus terminal. “We beat him to set an example that crime against women will be taken seriously and nobody else dares to commit such a crime,” police officer DP Unadkat said, according to the Times of India newspaper. “When we do this, they fear the police,” Unadkat said, The Indian Express reported . Some social media users praised the beating while others denounced the police officers’ actions, with several X users saying the man had yet to be found guilty of the crime. Bhavnagar police chief Nitesh Pandey told AFP only: “I have nothing to comment.”

Dar, Saudi and Turkish FMs follow up on understandings reached in first Makkah Defence Alliance meeting: FO. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar held phone calls with Saudi Arabian and Turkish foreign ministers on Sunday and followed up on the understandings reached at the inaugural meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance last month, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The joint defence pact was signed on August 7 and empowers the member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Its inaugural meeting was held on August 31 in Istanbul, where it was decided that the alliance’s secretariat would be initially headed by Pakistan for three years. The three countries also agreed to work towards strengthening their defence capabilities and the cohesion of their armed forces through joint activities, robust defence industry cooperation, and joint technology development and production. Moreover, through the institutionalised and resolute implementation of the Makkah agreement, the three countries also agreed to provide essential contributions to regional peace and stability. In a series of posts on social media platform X, FO said that DPM Dar held separate phone calls with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal Bin Farhan and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Sunday. In the call with the Saudi FM, the two leaders discussed regional and international developments, including matters of mutual interest at multilateral fora. “They also discussed follow-up on the understandings reached at the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee of the Makkah Defence Alliance, held in Istanbul, and agreed to remain in close contact,” FO said. In a separate post, FO said that Dar also spoke to Fidan and thanked him for hosting the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Istanbul. FO said the two leaders followed up on understandings reached and discussed ways to further advance cooperation under the framework. “The two foreign ministers also exchanged views on regional and international developments. They also discussed matters of mutual interest and opportunities to further strengthen cooperation at multilateral fora,” FO added. The tripartite agreement was signed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif during a summit at Al-Safa Palace. Pakistan has said that the pact is “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. And while Turkiye has said that there is a possibility of Egypt joining the pact, there has been no confirmation from Cairo. Abdelatty invites Dar Earlier in the day, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty invited DPM Dar to visit his country, FO said. A statement issued by the FO said that the two held a telephone call in which they exchanged views on Egypt-Pakistan bilateral relations and regional and international developments. Abdelatty invited Dar to “hold a bilateral visit to Egypt at his earliest convenience”, it added. They also reaffirmed their commitment to remaining “engaged and involved” on regional security matters, agreeing to meet on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) this month. Last November, the Egyptian foreign minister undertook an official two-day visit to Pakistan at DPM Dar’s invitation. During the visit, he met Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir at the General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, where the two discussed “defence and security cooperation, military exchanges, training collaborations and regional peace and stability”, FO said at the time. Abdelatty also met President Asif Ali Zardari during the visit. Pakistan and Egypt are also members of a quadrilateral regional alliance known as the R-4 Group (Regional Four), an arrangement which also includes Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. The R-4 group has been focused on regional security and emerged in March amid mediation efforts between the US and Iran.

PPP's Akhtar Abbas Nashad wins by-election in Skardu's GBA-09. GILGIT: PPP candidate Akhtar Abbas Nashad won the by-election in GBA-09 (Skardu-III) by a margin of 305 votes after a closely contested race, according to official results issued on Sunday. The constituency recorded an overall voter turnout of 51.79 per cent in the election held a day ago. According to the Form 47 issued on Sunday, Nashad received 8,399 votes while his opponent, independent candidate Wazir Saleem, received 8,094 votes. The by-election was held after the GB Supreme Appellate Court disqualified PPP candidate Fida Muhammad Nashad — Abbas’s father — who had been declared a returned candidate in the June general elections . In the by-election, Fida’s son entered the electoral fray and reclaimed the seat that had been lost by his father. The by-election concluded after a highly thrilling contest, marked by a fierce battle between the two candidates that persisted right up to the final stage. More than 800 police personnel, in addition to GB Scouts, were deployed under special security arrangements for the polling. The electoral process remained largely smooth and peaceful, while a local holiday was also declared to facilitate voters. Analysts had said a close contest was expected between PPP’s Abbas and independent candidate Saleem. They said Abbas could retain his father’s vote bank and may benefit from public sympathy following Nashad’s disqualification by the GB Supreme Appellate Court. District Returning Officer (DRO) Hamza Murad told Dawn on Friday that GBA-09 had 61 polling stations, of which 25 had been declared sensitive under Category A, 11 had been placed in Category B as medium-sensitive, and 25 had been classified as normal under Category C. With this seat, the PPP will hold 15 seats in the 33-seat Gilgit-Baltistan Assembly. Currently, the PPP has 14 seats, the PML-N has nine, the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party has six, and the Majlis Wahdat-i-Muslimeen and a PTI-backed independent occupy one seat each.

Scuffle in Karachi's DHA: Fresh case registered after inquiry report finds first FIR unsubstantiated. KARACHI: A resident of Karachi’s Defence Housing Authority (DHA) has sought action against her neighbours and police personnel for allegedly beating her in a fresh case registered in connection with a scuffle outside her apartment last month, it emerged on Sunday. The matter came to light when the CCTV footage of the physical altercation at an apartment building in DHA’s Phase 6 surfaced on social media last week. The footage showed police officials restraining a woman as another woman with a dumbbell attacked her. However, the initial first information report (FIR) of the incident was registered against the woman who was assaulted and her brother. But an inquiry report later said that the allegations in the FIR were “not substantiated” by the findings and also recommended departmental action against police officials involved in the incident. The report also said the first FIR should be disposed of, and subsequently, another was registered at the Darakhshan police station on September 5. In the second FIR, a copy of which is available with Dawn , the complainant said she was a resident of a third-floor apartment in DHA, Phase 6. The FIR quoted her as saying that on August 20 at 11:45pm, she was at her house with her brother and mother when a police officer rang the apartment’s doorbell and told her that her neighbour was calling them to the ground floor. Shortly after, the complainant continued, her neighbour came upstairs while hurling curses and started banging on the door. “When I opened the door, she dragged me by the hair, snatched my phone, and threw it down,” she alleged. “When my mother came out, she grabbed her by the hair as well and beat her,” the complainant claimed, adding that her neighbour then pinned her to a wall. The neighbour then went to her apartment and came back with her daughter and some police officials and “attempted to take away our phones, […] and her daughter, who was carrying a dumbbell, hit us”, she alleged. She further stated that she, along with her family, ran inside the house and called the police. “Meanwhile, the police officials outside broke the CCTV camera and later, the Darakhshan police broke into our house and took my and my brother’s cellphones away,” the FIR said. The complainant sought action against the suspects for “beating me, stealing our mobile phones and damaging the security camera”. The case was registered under Sections 147 (punishment for rioting), 148(rioting, armed with deadly weapon), 379 (punishment for theft), 427(mischief causing damage to the amount of fifty rupees), and 337A(i) (whoever, by doing any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC). Police official suspended Meanwhile, Darakhshan Police Sub-Inspector Imran Khan was suspended with pay on Sunday, pending an inquiry into his conduct in the DHA scuffle case. “He is shifted to PHQ Garden, South Zone Karachi, where he will attend daily roll call/parade, accordingly,” the suspension notice dated Sept 6 said, a copy of which is available with Dawn . A show-cause notice issued to Imran by South Investigation Superintendent of Police (SP) Touheed Rehman Memon observed that Khan had “failed to collect the tangible evidence, video footage of the incident and conduct [an] impartial investigation purely on merit”. His conduct reflected “a lack of professional diligence, negligence and dereliction of duty”, the notice stated, a copy of which is available with Dawn . Appropriate punishment for the negligence could include removal from service, the notice stated. An inquiry report into the incident had previously found that the investigating officer, identified as SIP Imran, had undertaken “no serious efforts” to collect evidence and did not independently apply his mind to investigate the case. CCTV In the CCTV footage of the incident, a woman can be seen rushing down a flight of stairs with a dumbbell in her hand and charging at another woman before using it to hit her. The video also showed two individuals in what appeared to be police uniforms restraining the woman being assaulted, and a man who came up the stairs shortly after and began arguing with the woman with the dumbbell. At one point, the man and woman being assaulted managed to go inside what appeared to be their home, following which the woman with a dumbbell and another man began banging on their door and yelling obscenities. At the end, a man in a shalwar kameez was seen using a weapon, provided by one of the people in uniform, to smash the CCTV camera. Inquiry report An inquiry report, which was issued on Friday, found that the incident was sparked by a parking dispute between the mother-in-law of Korangi Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Fida Hussain Janwari and another resident. It identified the police officials visible in the CCTV footage as constables Saqib and Haider Sultan. It further added that the plainclothes man who destroyed the CCTV camera in the footage was Constable Taimoor Ahmed, while the official who handed over his weapon for this purpose was Constable Amir Sohail. “All were detailed for duty at the private bungalow of the Korangi SSP,” it said, adding that strict departmental action should be taken against them. It further said that the on-the-spot arrests in the case without justifiable evidence by Darakhshan Station House Officer Rashid Ali and Assistant Sub-inspector Aftab Mangi were not justifiable and spoke of the officials’ “tilt towards the aggressive party”. It said that the investigating officer, identified as Sub Inspector Imran, also undertook “no serious efforts” to collect evidence and did not independently apply his mind to investigate the case. “Hence, all three officials of District South are recommended to be strictly proceeded against departmentally for miscarriage of justice,” it said. It further said that the “lapse of supervision and lack of control over his subordinates is evident on the part of the Korangi SSP”. It called for examining his overall conduct in light of Civil Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 2020 and to take further action in this regard. The report also said that an FIR should be registered against the SSP’s mother-in-law and her daughter and son, as well as the police officials present at the time of the incident, while the “victim family shall be encouraged to initiate legal action at free will against them”.

FO condemns mosque demolition in India's Uttar Pradesh, terms it part of 'drive to erase Islamic heritage'. Pakistan on Sunday condemned the demolition of a century-old mosque in India’s Uttar Pradesh, describing it as part of an “Islamophobic and Hindutva-driven campaign to erase the Islamic heritage” in the country. Responding to media queries regarding the demolition, Foreign Office (FO) spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan condemned the move and described it as “a reprehensible action against a historic Islamic place of worship”. He recalled that the demolition of the Babri Mosque in 1992 was an “enduring symbol of this ideology of religious intolerance, prejudice and hatred”. “Pakistan calls upon the international community to take immediate cognisance of the systematic persecution of Muslims by Indian authorities,” the statement said, highlighting the “continued desecration and destruction of their places of worship under state patronage”. Khan called for accountability of Indian authorities for actions against the religious freedom and cultural heritage of all minorities, particularly Muslims. According to The Indian Express , the mosque, which was located inside a Collectorate in Saharanpur, was demolished a day earlier. The demolition came three days after a district court had dismissed an appeal against an order holding that the structure stood on government land and was unauthorised. The September 2 order did not itself mention demolition. The Indian Express quoted mosque staff member Tanveer Ahmed as saying that the order was for eviction, not demolition. He claimed the mosque was around 150 years old, and maintained that the land was recorded in their names. All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen president and Hyderabad lawmaker Asaduddin Owaisi condemned the demolition and questioned whether the constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion applied to Muslims, NDTV reported. According to Owaisi, the mosque dated back to 1911, claiming that the Collectorate itself was constructed later. In 2024, the Akhonji mosque, which was over 600 years old, was razed to the ground without any prior notice in Delhi’s Mehrauli district. In 1992, a Hindu mob destroyed the famous Babri mosque, triggering riots that killed about 2,000 people across India, most of them Muslims.

PTI claims Hammad Azhar arrested in Punjab. The PTI on Sunday claimed that its leader Hammad Azhar has been arrested, denouncing the action as “political vengeance”. While police officials said they were unaware of his arrest, sources said the PTI leader was taken into custody in Multan in a case pertaining to the May 9, 2023 riots. Replying to a query, Multan Regional Police Officer (RPO) Usman Akram Gondal told Dawn that he was unaware of any arrest and did not have any information. According to reports circulating online, the PTI leader was handed over to the Lahore police over his alleged involvement in a May 9 case. However, Lahore Investigation Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Muhammad Naveed said that he had no confirmation about Azhar’s arrest or handover to Lahore police. In its statement, the PTI termed the former finance minister’s arrest “the worst example of political vengeance and fascism”. The party demanded that Azhar be immediately presented in court if there was a criminal case against him, his fundamental and legal rights be ensured, and the “series of political vengeance be halted”. “Hammad Azhar is being continuously targeted with retaliatory actions on political grounds. The government is recklessly using state power to suppress political opponents and silence the voice of PTI,” it alleged. Former opposition leader in NA, Omar Ayub, also claimed on X that Azhar has been arrested. “Strongly condemn this act,” the PTI leader wrote, alleging that the move aimed to “thwart” the party’s march planned for September 27. Moonis Elahi, son of PTI President Parvez Elahi, said Azhar had been arrested in “various false cases”. In April 2025, Azhar had stepped down as the president of the party’s Punjab chapter for the third time, after his two previous resignations were rejected . Azhar reappeared in public on May 22, 2024, a year after he had gone into hiding when the state launched a crackdown against the party leadership following the violent incidents of May 9. The PTI leader had evaded arrest by the Counter-Terrorism Department, which raided the PTI secretariat in Islamabad. A police spokesperson said at the time that Azhar is wanted in three separate cases by the capital police, including two registered with Ramna police and one filed in 2023 with the CTD.

Lamine Yamal hits double as perfect Barcelona thrash Valencia. Lamine Yamal struck twice for Barcelona as they demolished Valencia 5-0 on Sunday to maintain their 100 percent start in La Liga. The reigning champions moved three points clear at the top of La Liga, after Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid lost 1-0 at Real Betis on Friday. Fermin Lopez, Raphinha and Pedri were also on target for Hansi Flick’s swaggering visitors on a hot afternoon on Spain’s east coast. Yamal did not take part in the team training session on Saturday after a knock but showed no signs of it during a dazzling display against Carlos Corberan’s Los Che. Barcelona, the only team in the top flight to win their first four games, took control from the start to the upset of Valencia’s fans at a persistently bad-tempered Mestalla stadium. Yamal opened the scoring with a clever lofted finish in the sixth minute after Lopez dinked a superb ball over the top for the teenage star. The 19-year-old slammed home at the near post for what he thought was Barca’s second goal but the goal was disallowed for a tight offside after a VAR review. Lopez netted the second with a crisp finish in the 22nd minute after former Newcastle winger Anthony Gordon teed him up. Barcelona suffered a blow when Eric Garcia had to go off hurt midway through the first half after a collision with team-mate Rodri’s shoulder, on the midfielder’s first start since arriving this summer from Manchester City. Yamal fired narrowly wide and Lopez struck the post as Flick’s side continued to dominate. Barca goalkeeper Joan Garcia made a smart save to thwart Arnaut Danjuma at his near post before the break. Raphinha, starting again as the team’s centre-forward, tapped home his sixth goal of the season from close range after Lopez fed him. Valencia goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski saved from Rodri before Pedri netted Barcelona’s fourth after an exchange of passes with Dani Olmo. New arrival Gabriel Jesus came on for his Barca debut as a substitute in the final 10 minutes and sent a low effort just wide. Yamal stayed onside to collect another Olmo pass and put away Barca’s fifth and conclude a profitable afternoon for both the World Cup winner and the Catalan giants.

Germany's far-right AfD emerges as landslide winner in eastern state vote. Germany’s far-right AfD won a landslide victory in a key regional election Sunday in the ex-communist east, taking at least 44 per cent of the vote according to exit polls by two public broadcasters. “We have made history today,” said a jubilant Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old lead candidate of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt state. It was, however, too early to tell whether the AfD will have enough votes for an absolute majority that would allow it to govern a state alone for the first time. The centre-right CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz came a distant second, winning around 18.5pc, according to exit polls by broadcasters ARD and ZDF . Depending on the eventual count, the CDU’s state premier Sven Schulze would hope to still be able to form a new multi-party coalition to block the AfD from power. All major parties have so far maintained a “firewall” of non-cooperation with the Moscow-friendly AfD, whose state branch is categorised as “right-wing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. A first-ever AfD state government would be a shock for many in Germany, which has been at pains to atone for its dark history of World War II and the Holocaust and so far kept extremist parties at bay. The spectre of a far-right state government drew thousands of the AfD’s opponents to a rally on Saturday in Magdeburg, the regional capital, with banners saying “life is better without Nazis”. “I’m very worried,” demonstrator Laura Saalfeld told AFP . “Whatever the results, the atmosphere will change. Far-right sympathisers will show themselves more openly on the streets.” Smiling face, radical agenda Siegmund, the AfD’s telegenic top candidate, has ambitions to lead a political revolution from Saxony-Anhalt that would propel the party to national victory in 2029. On the campaign trail, Siegmund — a former entrepreneur with a sharp undercut hairstyle and a huge social media following — has been mobbed by adoring fans, many wearing T-shirts bearing his likeness. The party has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany as well as lingering resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall. In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth on Sunday in his hometown of Tangermünde. While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting irregular migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one. The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes vows to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard, and to change history teaching to lessen the emphasis on the Third Reich. In order to replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering “baby bonuses” for families to reverse the shrinking of the population in the small state of 2.1 million people. The German Economic Institute has warned the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector. Others have voiced fears that an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia, which Moscow could use to destabilise Germany. The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin”, Thuringia state interior minister Georg Maier told the Handelsblatt daily. The strong AfD win also heaps pressure on Merz , who has vowed to reboot a stagnant economy and restrict irregular immigration, but has seen his party beaten by the AfD in national surveys too. Political scientist Wolfgang Schroeder of Kassel University said that after an AfD win in Saxony-Anhalt, “Merz’s critics will become even more vocal, and calls for better leadership will become impossible to ignore”.

NA speaker's ruling on employee records cannot restrict citizen's right to information, PIC rules. ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Information Commission (PIC) has ruled that the National Assembly speaker’s decision to classify certain records cannot restrict citizens’ right to information (RTI) unless the ruling gives reasons showing that the harm from disclosure outweighs the public interest. The PIC issued the ruling while deciding two appeals filed by journalist Saddia Mazhar against the NA Secretariat. One of the appeals sought information about officers who had joined the NA Secretariat on deputation from January 2018 onwards, including their parent departments, grades, appointment dates, promotions and records relating to their induction into the secretariat. The NA Secretariat had argued that minutes of meetings, official file notes and recommendations relating to the employees had been classified under the speaker’s ruling of Oct 4, 2022, issued under the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the National Assembly, 2007 . The speaker’s ruling had declared various records, including committee minutes, briefing material, working papers and certain personal records of employees, as classified for the purposes of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017 . The PIC held that the speaker, being the head of the National Assembly Secretariat, could exercise the powers under Section 7(f) of the Right of Access to Information Act, despite the provision specifically referring to the minister-in-charge of a public body. However, the PIC stressed that such power was subject to the statutory requirements of the law. “[The] ruling does not contain reasons as to why the harm from disclosure of information outweighs the public interest,” the PIC observed, concluding that it therefore could not operate to classify the records. It further held that the speaker’s ruling was neither prospectively nor retrospectively operative because it failed to meet the legal criteria required for classification under Section 7(f) of the Act. Regarding the employees’ records sought by the applicant, it noted that appointment and promotion notifications were already published in the official Gazette. It therefore found no legal basis for withholding the information. The PIC also dismissed the secretariat’s preliminary objections regarding the non-provision of a copy of the applicant’s computerised national identity card (CNIC) and her non-appearance in person, declaring both grounds legally unsustainable under the Act. It noted that information already published in the official Gazette or otherwise publicly accessible cannot be withheld. The commission directed the NA’s deputy secretary, or a designated officer, to provide the applicant with a specific link to information available on the secretariat’s website and furnish certified copies of the remaining requested information, including Gazette-notified records, within 10 days of receiving the order. The ruling also emphasised that the 2017 RTI Act takes precedence over inconsistent provisions contained in other laws under Section 25 of the Act. In a 2025 policy brief, the Free and Fair Election Network (Fafen) noted that the RTI regime in Pakistan was stifled by institutional inertia and deep-rooted secrecy norms despite advanced legal provisions. It had called for comprehensive legal reforms to strengthen the implementation of the RTI law.

Iran warns of 'more painful response' if US launches further attacks. Iran’s top negotiator on Sunday threatened a more forceful response to any further US attacks after Tehran targeted American warships in their latest round of clashes. The exchanges of fire, which began with US raids last week, come amid a deadlock in the six-month war between the two foes. Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Washington is also seeking to choke Iran’s economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the country in a bid to force it into submission. “The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end,” said Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war. “Any aggression against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response,” he added, in a speech carried by state media. On Saturday, US Central Command (Centcom), which oversees American military operations in the region, said Iran had unsuccessfully fired at two American warships — an aircraft carrier and a destroyer. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said the warships had been “forced to retreat” after “suffering damage”, but Centcom said they successfully evaded the attacks. In response, the US military said it struck three oil tankers linked to the Iranian Guards. Centcom said it had “permanently disabled” one ship off the coast of the oil hub of Kharg Island and another near Jask, and “completely destroyed” a third vessel in the Gulf of Oman. Video posted by the military showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships. The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies”, Centcom said. Iran quickly retaliated, with the Guards saying their naval forces “targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas”. It warned ships not to attempt to transit the key trade waterway via routes unapproved by Tehran. Early on Sunday, Iran’s IRGC also said it attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television. Centcom spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins, however, called the claim “a complete lie”. “No US vessels have been attacked today,” he said. ‘Clinging on to power’ Centcom commander Admiral Brad Cooper had said after the exchange of strikes: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours.” The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the attacks on its oil tankers as “illegal and aggressive actions”. The administration of US President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near. US Vice President JD Vance has gone so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war”. Trump reiterated that view on Friday, calling the war “small potatoes” for Washington. Iranian officials have so far maintained their defiant tone, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told ABC ’s “This Week” programme on Sunday that Iran was “doing everything they can to cling on to something”. “They know their nuclear programme’s coming to an end. Their navy has come to an end. Their air force has come to an end. They’re clinging on to power,” he said. A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed. Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as “new US territory”. Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in the strait.

Pakistan dispatches humanitarian aid to Nepal after deadly floods, landslides. Pakistan on Sunday dispatched 100 tonnes of humanitarian assistance to Nepal to support relief efforts following the recent deadly floods and landslides. The glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,384 people and left more than 5,500 missing across the two countries. In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,341 bodies, while around 4,996 people remain missing. The humanitarian aid from Pakistan was coordinated by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and sent by a chartered flight from Islamabad to Kathmandu, the Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement. “The relief consignment comprised tents, blankets, mats, hygiene kits and medicines for the affected communities,” FO said. The send-off ceremony for the humanitarian assistance was held at the Islamabad airport, and was attended by Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, Nepal’s Ambassador Rita Dhital, along with senior FO and NDMA officials. “The assistance reflects Pakistan’s solidarity with the government and people of Nepal during this difficult time,” FO noted. Sharing the development on X, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said: “Our thoughts and prayers are with the bereaved families and all those affected. Pakistan stands in solidarity with the Government and people of Nepal and remains ready to extend all possible support in this difficult hour.” In a post late on Sunday night, the NDMA said the humanitarian assistance for the flood-affected people of Nepal had been “handed over to relevant authorities”. Rescue operations continue In Nepal, rescuers faced challenging conditions on Sunday as search operations after catastrophic floods entered a 12th day, buoyed by the extraordinary rescues of four survivors. Rescuers found two more people alive on Saturday, joining two saved the day before in what have been described as miraculous tales of survival. Three of those have been found in hydropower tunnels where the government initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive. “Search and rescue is going on at the tunnels despite geography, adverse weather and lack of connectivity,” Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha told AFP . Rescue workers were experiencing “multiple challenges”, he said. The wall of icy water and debris tore through mountain districts on August 26, destroying roads, bridges and other infrastructure. On Saturday, rescuers pulled a Chinese man alive from deep inside a hydropower tunnel, and a 64-year-old Nepali woman, Chandrika Shrestha, from her mud-covered home. Nepal Police officers assist Chandrika Kumari Shrestha after she was rescued alive from a damaged house following deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Betrawati in Nuwakot district, Nepal on Sept 5, 2026. —Nepal Police/Handout via Reuters Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the latter rescue had “given hope to the entire nation”. A day earlier, two Nepali hydropower workers were rescued at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, where searches continue alongside multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects affected. Other examples of remarkable fortitude have emerged from Nepal, including Rajendra Dawadi, a school principal who quickly ordered an evacuation as the torrent approached, saving hundreds of students’ lives. “If the information was wrong, we would lose a day of schooling,” he told AFP . “But if it was true, we were going to lose our lives.” Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said work was continuing to restore electricity in several areas. “Places that have unreachable, we’ve tried to restore power with solar,” he told AFP . Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has called the disaster a “Himalayan tsunami” and has warned reconstruction costs could run into the billions of dollars. The United Nations has said the magnitude of the destruction makes delivering aid an immense challenge, and has launched a $50 million appeal to help more than 84,000 people. With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves, after taking DNA samples for future identification, according to the police. Only around 100 bodies have been identified and handed over to families. Nepal will hold a national day of mourning on Monday, the 13th day since the disaster, in line with a traditional period of mourning in Hindu rituals. While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melting worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

FWO seeks 4-year payback for $432m Azeri-funded pipeline. • Guaranteed transportation tariff to facilitate Socar participation • Pipeline tariff projected at $64 a tonne • Project to link Faisalabad, Thalian and Tarujabba ISLAMABAD: Supported by the federal government, the Frontier Works Organisation (FWO) has sought recovery of about $432 million in investment in the proposed 437km Faisalabad-Peshawar white oil pipeline within four years through a guaranteed transportation tariff to ensure the participation of Socar, Azerbaijan’s state oil company. Under a tariff petition filed with the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra), transportation of petroleum products from Faisalabad to Thalian near Rawalpindi and onward to Tarujabba near Peshawar would cost about $64 per tonne in the first year, targeted for 2029, before gradually declining to $14.5 per tonne by 2058, the final year of the proposed 30-year tariff period. Ogra has published the 3,033-page tariff petition along with the Front-End Engineering Design, volume stability report and financial model before formally approving the tariff, which has already received backing of the Economic Coordination Com­m­ittee and cabinet to satisfy Socar. An official said Ogra was expected to approve the construction-stage tariff soon. Frontier Oil Company (FOC) — a subsidiary of FWO, Pakistan State Oil and Socar — told the regulator that while capital expenditure on the Faisalabad-Thalian-Tarujabba White Oil Pipeline would be substantially higher than road transportation, the pipeline tariff had been structured to decline over time as capital costs were depreciated or amortised and debt was repaid. The project is proposed to have a 55:45 debt-to-equity ratio. FOC said the declining tariff would pass the benefit of lower costs to consumers over time, in contrast with road transportation costs, which tended to increase. The project is considered important for strategic and national reasons and would transport both petrol and high-speed diesel from Gatti in Faisalabad to Tarujabba, completing a pipeline “backbone” from Karachi to Peshawar. It is intended to meet increasing petroleum demand in northern parts of the country, including demand linked to CPEC-related development and increasing vehicle ownership, while reducing the risk of recurring fuel shortages. The project is also expected to improve the reliability and safety of supplies to northern Punjab and Pes­h­awar, reduce dependence on road tankers and lower carbon emissions. The project is expected to rely largely on local resources while providing dollar-linked returns allowing recovery of the investment in four years. The ministries of finance and power had raised objections to such an upfront return on investment. The proposed pipeline comprises a 256km, 20-inch line from Faisalabad to Thalian, with capacity of about seven million tonnes per annum, extendable to 10m tonnes. A 172km, 12-inch section would run from Thalian to Tarujabba with capacity of 5m tonnes per annum, while an 8-inch, 9km spur would connect Thalian to Faqirabad. The estimated cost has been put at $320m for the first section, $94m for the second and $17.5m for the third. Ogra has assessed the project life at 30 years. Interestingly, the project cost approved by the ECC about five months ago had been $300m and the two ministries had expressed reservations over guaranteed dollar-based returns on petroleum transportation. The proposed pipeline is to be developed on a government-to-government basis with Socar, FWO and PSO through a joint project company. The project, now being treated as a strategic investment from Azerbaijan, had earlier been pursued by FWO through local resources. Power Minister Awais Leghari had cautioned against guaranteed dollar-based returns. He argued all aspe­cts of the investment proposal, incl­uding project cost and internal rate of return, should be thoroughly chec­ked in light of the IPP experience. Socar had sought a “ship or pay” arrangement for its investment, similar to the “take or pay” mechanism used in power purchase agreements, under which payment would be made for committed pipeline capacity even if the petroleum products were not transported for some reason. The finance ministry also questioned the proposed four-year payback period, arguing that dollarised returns should apply only where foreign investment actually materialised and should not be extended to locally financed investment. It sought rationalisation of interest-rate assumptions and weighted average cost of capital. It proposed extending the payback period to seven years to reduce the tariff burden in the project’s early years. The ministry also wanted the petroleum division, rather than Ogra, to finalise technical issues related to the Inland Freight Equalisation Margin and the declaration of the pipeline as the default mode of transportation. However, the petroleum division argued that such changes would make the project unattractive. Therefore, the ECC overruled the finance ministry’s demand for revised payouts as well as the power minister’s reservations, observing that the project could open new avenues for investment and should be viewed in “a larger strategic perspective” and be understood as an investment opportunity. At present, about 70pc of petrol and diesel is transported by road, 28pc through the existing pipeline network from Karachi to Machike and 2pc by rail. The new project is expected to increase the share of petroleum products transported by pipeline by around 10pc. The tariff would be denominated in US dollars and linked to optimal utilisation of pipeline capacity under a “default mode of transportation”. Under the proposed mechanism, oil marketing companies would be required to commit minimum annual pipeline volumes and any shortfall would be covered through the Inland Freight Equalisation Margin. According to the agreed mechanism, Ogra will design a regulatory framework to ensure optimal utilisation of pipeline by declaring it a default mode of transportation. Given high stakes and quick returns, Ogra was previously nervous about taking a regulatory stance and instead wanted the ECC to provide comfort zone with clearance on key terms and conditions submitted by the FWO and agreed between stakeholders for the project. Inflation as a fiscal problem. Amid the post-Covid 19 massive inflationary spiral, the fiscally suffocated government, with limited days of foreign exchange reserves, became dependent on the domestic debt market to finance its massive deficits amid rising inflation. Therefore, it had to issue a massive amount of floating-rate, long-tenor debt instruments to manage extreme rollover risk. For reference, the total cumulative issuance of semi-annual floating Pakistan Investment Bonds increased from less than Rs1 trillion in 2020 to more than Rs14tr in 2024, and is currently more than Rs22tr. Floating rate instruments constitute approximately 70 per cent of all domestic sovereign debt. The debt portfolio’s Average Time to Maturity (ATM) is near 3.9 years, while Average Time to Refix (ATR) stands just above one year. This leads to a vicious cycle of repricing: price increases immediately upset fiscal accounts. The conventional economic theory believes price spirals are the result of excess aggregate demand that the State Bank of Pakistan can tame by raising interest rates. However, Pakistan has high cost-push, structural, and import-driven inflation. The recurring price spirals are mainly on the supply side and are the result of sudden currency devaluation, global commodity shocks, frequent revisions of administered energy tariffs to offset energy sector circular debt and domestic food supply bottlenecks. In this structural context, the monetary policy measures taken by the State Bank of Pakistan are certainly needed. In the absence of a hawkish monetary policy amid an inflationary wave, inflationary expectations quickly get out of hand, second-round wage-price spirals set in, and exchange rate pressures build up, potentially leading to an uncontained macroeconomic spiral. But the central bank’s tightening directly affects the most important channel that links inflation to an overwhelming fiscal burden: the domestic cost of debt. The government should continue to work on structural reprofiling to address the sovereign portfolio’s repricing sensitivity The correlation between debt servicing and headline inflation in the period 2006-16 was negligible and became moderate to strong post the 2022-23 spiral. The central bank’s rate hike to tackle price shocks reprices the government’s huge domestic floating debt stock. This means that the policy rate hikes get quickly and vigorously passed on through the sovereign debt portfolio to fiscal expenditures. This transmission is a delayed pass-through, with the sensitivity of debt servicing being highest after two to three quarters as floating instruments reprice at successive auctions. The costs of servicing the debt take up a large share of the federal budget. Despite three consecutive years of contractionary fiscal policy delivering consistent primary surpluses, debt servicing consumes 40 per cent of the federal budget. The government had no choice but to cut development spending and investment in productive capital. An anti-price policy, used to control prices, ends up increasing fiscal pressure, deteriorating the composition of public finances, and consuming public investments that can no longer be used for long-term structural productivity spending. This structural problem would need to be significantly addressed by improving sovereign debt indicators. The Debt Management Office has achieved good results in the past few years, with its efforts to reprofile domestic maturities, increase fixed-rate debt issuances, and extend the average maturity of the public debt stock. However, the sovereign portfolio is still quite sensitive to repricing risk. Added to these fiscal weaknesses are the severe climate and geopolitical vulnerabilities facing Pakistan. It is still one of the most climate-sensitive countries in the world and continues to suffer from devastating floods, heatwaves, and yield losses that displace millions of people, destroy infrastructure, trigger food inflation, and erode fiscal buffers. The current adaptation and mitigation actions are not adequate in view of the magnitude of the challenge. There is an urgent need to build dedicated infrastructure for climate change adaptation, modernise water management, improve storage logistics, and make agriculture climate-smart in Pakistan to reduce vulnerability to frequent environmental shocks. At the same time, Pakistan has to deal with its extreme geoeconomic vulnerabilities in a fracturing global order. The domestic economy is highly vulnerable to cross-border commodity price fluctuations, given its high reliance on imported fuel. The geopolitical and climate vulnerabilities have resulted in stagflationary pressures, leading to severe episodes of macroeconomic instability. The need to protect the economy requires proactive fiscal measures to overcome acute climate and geopolitical vulnerabilities, as recurring price spirals are not the result of runaway domestic demand but of price disruptions from outside the economy. State agencies need to invest in climate-smart agricultural infrastructure, streamline storage logistics, and limit dependence on imported energy to shield the real economy from likely and unpredictable supply-side shocks. The Debt Management Office, on the other hand, should continue working on structural reprofiling, which involves increasing the proportion of fixed-rate debt and lengthening debt maturities, to address the sovereign portfolio’s repricing sensitivity. The government has to address these structural and debt-market fault lines, so that conventional monetary interventions will no longer exacerbate the sovereign’s fiscal difficulties. Khanzaib Ahmad is a co-developer of the Monetary Policy Uncertainty Index for Pakistan and an analyst at Chase Securities. Abdul Moeez Mirza is a research assistant at IBA School of Business Studies Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, September 7th, 2026

Defiant KP CM reaches Karachi on last leg of Sindh drive. • Afridi asks Punjab CM to ‘apologise’ over controversial remarks against other provinces • PTI shifts rally venue from Mazar-i-Quaid to Toll Plaza amid restrictions; youth asked to join Sept 27 campaign • Karachi mayor says PTI free to come to city if it follows the law KARACHI/HYDERABAD: After a journey of more than six hours, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi finally reached the Karachi Toll Plaza in the early hours of Monday, with his convoy negotiating blockades, dug-up roads, and other hurdles that the party alleged were placed by the government to stop or delay his arrival. The long-awaited arrival of the CM Afridi-led caravan from Hyderabad and Umerkot triggered scenes of celebration at the Toll Plaza where a crowd of PTI supporters, including women and children, had gathered to welcome them as fireworks lit up the night sky and jubilant workers raised slogans in their support. The chief minister was accompanied by PTI Sindh president Haleem Adil Sheikh and other party leaders on the last leg of his five-day public mobilisation campaign in Sindh for the Sept 27 nationwide protest call to demand the hospitalisation and release of incarcerated ex-premier Imran Khan. Before leaving Hyderabad for Karachi on Sunday evening, CM Afridi had accused the Sindh government of creating hurdles in his march and vowed that he would not leave the province without launching the ‘free Imran Khan’ movement with his rally in the port city. “If we cannot reach Karachi today, God willing, we will hold the rally tomorrow; if not tomorrow, then the day after. I will not take a single step out of Sindh without launching a street movement in Karachi. I will stay here until the objective is achieved.” The PTI, however, had to change the venue of its planned rally from Mazar-i-Quaid to the Karachi Toll Plaza to ensure that the leadership and workers could reach the gathering. PTI’s Sindh chapter spokesperson Muhammad Ali Baloch alleged that containers, vehicles and other barriers had been placed along the route leading to Mazar-i-Quaid, besides at several locations at the Kotri bridge. He said PTI workers from across Karachi had gathered at the Toll Plaza, where the party had prepared a stage and a truck for the gathering. Separately, Karachi’s District East police, in a statement, said that “no public gatherings, rallies or processions will be allowed around Mazar-i-Quaid”. ‘No dispute over gathering’ Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab, who is also a spokesman for the Sindh government rejected the allegations that the arrangements were specifically aimed at PTI and said the party was free to come to the metropolitan city provided it followed the law. He told the media there was no disagreement with PTI members over the gathering, but warned that “no one should take the law into their own hands”. He said the administration routinely makes security and traffic arrangements, including placing containers and imposing restrictions on roads, whenever a large political gathering takes place. The mayor was responding to the allegations levelled by the PTI that the Sindh government had erected roadblocks to prevent the party’s convoy from reaching Karachi for the rally. Speaking from the convoy’s route, the party’s Sindh chapter president Haleem Adil Sheikh said the CM and other leaders were travelling through “remote and deserted” rural roads after facing repeated obstructions and vowed that PTI workers would reach Karachi despite the restrictions. “We are removing the barriers and moving forward. Karachi, wait for us, we are coming,” he said. He claimed that the convoy had been held up for around four hours en route to Karachi from Hyderabad and alleged that officials had removed their vehicle’s tyres while police took away its driver. Rally in Hyderabad Earlier, addressing a gathering in Hyderabad, the KP CM lashed out at the Punjab chief minister for making a controversial statement against smaller provinces, wherein she said Punjab faced internal threats instead of threats from across the border. “Punjab CM should tender an apology for her statement,” he said, while also seeking a “clarification” from the Pakistan Army’s media spokesperson. Addressing the ISPR director general, he said, “You tell us that India is our enemy but the one you got elected is saying India is not a threat to her. Please tell us who is right?” He also said only two families were ruling Pakistan — one from Sindh and the other from Punjab — but it was only the PTI whose leader Imran Khan picked an ordinary worker like him as the chief minister. He said the PTI’s mandate was stolen in the Feb 2024 elections. The KP CM also urged the youth to stand up for the country and for themselves because the future belonged to them. He also urged them to join the Sept 27 movement. “Will you join us on Sept 27 because people say there will be bullets? I am ready for it and are you ready?” he roared. Earlier, he addressed a rally at Allah Wala Chowk in Umerkot, where he arrived six hours behind schedule. He called upon his party supporters to come out on Sept 27 if the PTI faced repression, saying they had to stand firm for their future and that of their children. A.B. Arisar in Umerkot also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, September 7th, 2026

President’s London tour sets tongues wagging. ISLAMABAD: Amid the ongoing debate over the creation of new provinces and the PPP’s outright rejection of the proposal, President Asif Ali Zardari’s extended presence in London has raised questions about the political dimensions of the tour, particularly when Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who had recently floated the idea, is also in the UK. While some believe the president travelled to Lon­don solely for a medical check-up, others view the visit as a political move aimed at putting pressure on the government. An official video clip of Mr Naqvi’s meeting with President Zardari also generated discussion about the president’s position. After all, it was the interior minister who ignited the fresh debate through his diatribe about the collapse of the existing governance sys­tem, and called for a ‘reset’. Following his London sojourn, Mr Naqvi rece­ntly doubled down on his dem­and for new administrative units. Addressing a National Policy Dia­logue on ‘Devol­ution of Powers and Good Governance in Pakistan’ at the University of Management and Tech­n­o­logy on Saturday, Mr Naqvi clarified that his proposed “reset” did not mean a change of government or political party, rather a comprehensive review and restructuring of the administrative system to make it responsive to the needs of citizens. He even called for a debate on granting provincial status to Islamabad, saying residents of the federal capital did not receive a share under the National Finance Commission (NFC) award. ‘Apolitical’ trip The president’s meeting with the interior minister was followed by gatherings of senior PPP leaders with Mr Zardari in London and, subsequently, the passage of a resolution by the Sindh Assembly rejecting the creation of new provinces. The sequence of events has led to speculation that the PPP’s position was discussed during the London meetings and that the Sindh Assembly resolution was adopted with the president’s consent. The issue of President Zardari’s ‘Euro trip’ and his meeting with the interior minister and Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar was also raised at last week’s Foreign Office briefing. However, the FO spokesperson did not respond, instead referring the question to the Presidency. When contacted, President Zardari’s spokesperson Murtaza Solangi told Dawn he was unaware of the details of the president’s visit, or when he would return to the country. “It is solely a private visit. I never seek details of his private visits,” he said. PPP Secretary General Nayyar Hussain Bokhari also maintained that the president had travelled to London only for a medical check-up and that there was nothing political about the trip. Responding to a question about Mr Zardari’s meeting with Mr Naqvi, he said the interior minister had maintained a close association with the president for a long time. “There was nothing serious if the minister met Zardari sahib to inquire about his health,” he said. Another PPP source, however, confirmed that the president’s visit had reasons beyond his medical treatment. PPP leaders meet Zardari The source said that PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla and Dr Asim Hussain, considered close confidants of the president, also joined him later in the UK. “President Zardari has conveyed a clear message to the government through passage of a resolution in Sindh Assembly that he and his party ruling in Sindh reject any plan to create new provinces,” the source said. According to the source, the PPP had initially agreed in principle to the creation of two new provinces in Punjab — south Punjab and Bahawalpur — but changed its position after the government began considering the creation of new federating units in all four existing provinces. The party subsequently opposed the broader proposal, and has recently questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence on the politically sensitive issue of creating new provinces and sought a clear position from him. The party had initially not opposed the idea of creating additional federating units, but insisted that any such move should be undertaken in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Constitution. Now, it is openly opposing the proposal, with the PPP-led Sindh government securing passage of a resolution in the provincial assembly rejecting any further division of the country’s four existing provinces. The development is politically significant because, although the PML-N-led government enjoys a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly, it relies on PPP support. If the PPP withdraws that support, imp­lementing any constitutional amendment aimed at creating new provinces would become considerably more difficult. IPP chief slams govt Adding to the growing criticism from within the ruling coalition, Comm­uni­cations Minister Abdul Aleem Khan, who belongs to another government ally, the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party (IPP), also criticised the government on Sunday over what he described as its poor performance. He said people were not being provided with basic necessities and that no one who genuinely loved the country could be satisfied with the existing system. Mr Khan pointed to shortages of clean drinking water, deteriorating hospitals and the large number of children deprived of education. He also highlighted the poor condition of schools across the country. In a message on X, Mr Khan said people remained deprived of basic facilities while their hardships were increasing day by day. “If the provinces were delivering effectively under the existing system, why would the people be in such a condition?” he asked. He said there was a need to set aside prejudice and examine the actual condition of the people, arguing that the public was frustrated and deprived of basic amenities. Situationer: From jammers to drones — KP’s fight against terrorists ‘takes flight’. FROM handheld jammers to anti-drone systems, and now a specialised human division trained for Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) combat, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) police department is waging a high-tech war against terrorists as their threat evo­lves from quadcopter surveillance and ammunition drops to swarm attacks. The UAV division, initially floated as an idea, was established following technological advancements in terrorist capabilities and their shifting preference from conventional street fighting to aerial warfare. Trained in modern drone flying, aerial surveillance, intelligence gathering, counterterrorism, protection of sensitive installations, and the effective use of UAV technology in high-risk operations, the division is the first of its kind established by a police department in the country. Ambushes and attacks on police installations are still reported from across the province, but terrorists are also using quadcopters for surveillance before moving towards their targets, enabling them to avoid ambushes by law enforcement agencies. “This is a fact that they fly surveillance drones before targeting any installation of the law enforcement agencies,” a senior official said. Changing tactics, external backing Senior officials also believe that the situation has completely changed from what it was two years ago, as terrorists’ tactics have evolved, compelling the police force to devise a fresh strategy to stay one step ahead. They said that with drones being deployed and law enforcement facilities being targeted, the war had expanded to the skies, forcing them into a technological arms race, particularly in high-risk zones. “It is a fact that the terrorists are more equipped than police since they got hold of the leftover [modern gadgets left behind by the US and its allies in Afghanistan],” a senior security official said while talking to Dawn . He said the local threat was previously underdeveloped and pointed to continued ‘external’ support — in the form of manpower, finances and technology. He added that the use of quadcopters for surveillance followed by explosive delivery required financial resources, training and, above all, technology. The department responded immediately, but the handheld anti-drone guns could neutralise only one drone at a time. This gave the police an edge, but it was soon the terrorists’ turn to adapt. After realising the weakness, they turned to swarm tactics, deploying multiple drones simultaneously. Again, the department took another step by upgrading its defensive capabilities and investing in anti-drone systems capable of detecting and jamming multiple quadcopters at the same time. With anti-drone systems deployed in multiple areas across the province, quadcopter attacks dropped sharply. The department did not give militants the opportunity to gain another advantage and moved to establish an entire division specialising in aerial warfare. Data centre, skills training Officials said the KP police realised that technology alone could not help and took a crucial step by establishing a specialised division of personnel trained for UAV operations. These personnel are not only trained to operate drones for surveillance but are also capable of conducting electronic warfare against hostile UAVs. They said a data centre based in Peshawar would receive real-time information on quadcopters and, at the same time, coordinate the response of law enforcement agencies. “The war is escalating and the threat has changed. What we see today is completely different from what we saw two years ago,” KP police chief Zulfiqar Hameed told Dawn , explaining why, beyond technological development, trained human operators were equally critical. Mr Hameed said the specialised unit was the need of the hour and that, besides deploying it in the provincial capital, the department had approved similar units at the district level, initially in high-risk districts. He said the department had deployed drones across the province and that not only the regular police but also the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) would be equipped with more advanced drones — long-range models capable of flying at higher altitudes than the existing ones. These would be used against terrorists. “There is no other option for the future but technological advancement,” the KP police chief said. A new dark age?. RECENT years have seen a surge of books and articles on the impact of technology on people’s lives and thinking. While communication technology has opened new vistas and opportunities it has also created its own problems in our digital age. Some works celebrate its benefits. Others warn of its damaging consequences especially those of social media. James Marriott’s The New Dark Ages: The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society joins this debate from another angle. The British journalist’s work falls within the genre that emphasises the harmful consequences of digital technology. The book’s principal concern is that people aren’t reading anymore and that a screen culture is displacing a print culture. For Marriott, the spread of literacy and the kind of thinking nurtured by the world of print drove progress in economic development, scientific advancement, and the emergence of modern democracy. In a print culture, he argues, knowledge is organised, understood, and contextualised. “Books make arguments, propose theses and develop ideas.” This process, he contends, develops the power of reasoning. For Marriott, this is getting lost in an era where the smartphone has taken over our lives and become the main reason for the decline of reading. There has never been a technology quite like the smartphone, which has so much distracting content that it keeps people’s attention endlessly on the screen. He maintains that a hostile environment for learning has been created by this digital distraction. Screens are changing human behaviour. Smartphones are shaping a “fragmented, trivialised and angry new world”, in which conspiracy theories and mad ideas are spread at terrifying speed. The spread of knowledge is impeded by this and is actually breaking down. Political discourse once grounded in logical argument now takes place “amid the moronic inferno of social media”. Marriot attributes much of the 21st century’s disorder and unreason to the fading of the written word and the “colonisation of culture” by addictive screens. He sees the intellectual hollowing of society as a consequence of the decline of reading and the world becoming a less rational place. Public discourse today, he claims, has become trivial to the point of dysfunction. It has affected politics too as this environment encourages the rise of mediocre politicians with little understanding of history, whose appeals to the public are emotional and do not rest on rational propositions. Politics, Marriott argues, is growing “angrier, stupider and more obsessed with personality”. He laments the fact that the full ramifications of the onset of what he calls a post-literate society are not fully understood. Marriot may be overstating his case and exaggerating the damaging impact of digital technology. But he is no outlier in this assessment. Last year in a compelling book Superbloom: How Technologies of Connection Tear Us Apart , Nicholas Carr surveyed how digital technology — including smartphones, the internet, social media and artificial intelligence — is transforming both people and societies. He argued that instead of broadening minds, expanding empathy and fostering harmony, this technology has had the opposite effect. It is eroding understanding and trust and contributing to strife and social disharmony. Communication technology offers immense opportunities but has serious unintended consequences. For Carr, speed and intensity in the flow of information and stimuli compel people to rely on intuitive thinking based on biases. It deprives them of the ability to tap into deeper analysis. As a result, it has undermined reasoned analysis, methodical evaluation and contemplative inquiry. As he puts it “Attention splinters, understanding grows thin”. This results in mental shortcuts and shallow thinking. Thus “rather than levelling barriers to knowledge, it becomes a barrier itself”. For both Marriott and Carr, the information spread through digital vehicles does not foster knowledge but detracts from it. “More informed does not mean better informed.” The fragmented nature of information provided by the screen makes much of it useless, according to Marriott. Social media further dumbs down the public conversation. Marriott sees social media and short-form videos producing junk content and misleading posts. He also finds a connection between video platforms like TikTok and increased vote share for populist and far right parties. That’s because feeds by such parties play on emotions and abjure reasoning. Carr’s book devotes far more attention to social media. His criticism is unsparing. He also takes tech companies to task. In his view, social media amplifies falsehoods and hostility rather than promote facts and truth. Because it is shorn of communication barriers, it brings out people’s worst instincts. He also blames the “ugly content that pervades the social media” on tech companies and on algorithms. As he puts it, “Social media churns out information that’s been highly processed to stimulate not just engagement but also dependency.” By encouraging excessive and unchecked self-exposure to a mass audience, it shatters all boundaries. The result is discord, not harmony. An earlier book also warned of a world of fractured attention. In The Lonely Century , economist Noreena Hertz had a different focus, but she also addressed the harmful effects of communication technology and social media. She assigned a central role to social media and smartphones in making people “more angry and tribal”. Drawing on research, she argued that technology and social media were also fuelling a global loneliness crisis, both personal and political. Smartphones “fragment our attention”, estrange us from people and “create a splintered self”. Hertz saw social media trapping people into isolated digital bubbles and creating a meaner, more aggressive world. This is evident in trolling and other forms of online abuse. As a result, she urged the acknowledgement of the dangers of “tech addiction” and making social media platforms accountable. Communication technology has brought immense benefits to society. At the same time, it has involved serious unintended consequences. Where there is promise there is also peril. Managing the negative effects of new technologies remains a difficult challenge without easy solutions. With artificial intelligence the risk is even greater as it is growing much faster than our ability to control it. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
